title: The crying baby
hook: Shneur Zalman leaves his prayer to rock a crying baby his absorbed son never heard

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kotzker said God lives wherever people let Him in. Your line was wherever you let him in. Did you open a door, even a crack? Day three hundred six.

You've seen it. Someone so deep in their laptop they don't hear their name called three times. A parent on the phone while a toddler tugs and tugs at their sleeve. Or maybe that someone was you. Deep focus is a gift. It's how books get written and problems get solved. But it has a shadow. Today's story is about a great scholar, lost in holy study, who missed a sound that mattered more, and about his father, who didn't.
screen: `DEEP IN THE LAPTOP.` → `A TODDLER TUGGING A SLEEVE.` → `FOCUS HAS A SHADOW.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi founded the Chabad movement and wrote the Tanya, the book at its heart. The story is told that he lived in a house with his son, Dov Ber, who would later lead Chabad after him. One night Dov Ber was downstairs, completely absorbed in study. In the same room, his baby fell out of the cradle and began to cry. Dov Ber didn't hear a thing. Upstairs, Shneur Zalman was deep in his own study and prayer. He heard the crying. He stopped, came down the stairs, picked the baby up, soothed the child, and laid it back in the cradle. His son never looked up. Afterward, the father spoke to him. However lofty your learning, he said, if it keeps you from hearing a child cry, something has gone wrong. Notice who is doing the teaching here. Not a critic of study. The founder of a movement built on deep, intense contemplation. He isn't saying stop learning. He's saying learning that makes you deaf to a crying child has lost its way. The Talmud says something in the same spirit: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, based on Abraham leaving God's company to run to three strangers. Holiness that can't hear a baby isn't finished yet.
screen: `SHNEUR ZALMAN, FOUNDER OF CHABAD.` · `A SON TOO ABSORBED TO HEAR.` · `A FATHER WHO COMES DOWNSTAIRS.` · `LEARNING THAT HEARS.` · then, large: `THE CRYING CHILD FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for one small need. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, listen. Not to your thoughts. To the room. The sounds outside. Someone in the next room. A pet. Your own body: are you thirsty, tired, tense? Let each sound register. Now think of the people around you today. Who might be tugging at your sleeve, quietly, and you haven't noticed? Pick one. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
The crying baby. Shneur Zalman stopped his own holy study to comfort a child his son never heard. Holiness that hears.
Your line: the crying child first. Today, when someone needs you while you're busy with something important, stop, and look up. The work will wait. Day three hundred six.

howItsDone: Chabad Hasidim tell this story about their first and second rebbes, and it is retold in Jewish homes and schools as a reminder that study and prayer should not make a person deaf to others.

fork.reveal: Shneur Zalman stops, goes down, and soothes the child himself. then he tells his son: learning that can't hear a crying child has gone wrong.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a distracted dad.
what it means: holiness that can't hear someone in need isn't finished.
what a scholar hears: told of the first two Chabad rebbes, it echoes the Talmud's teaching (Shabbat 127a) that hospitality outranks receiving the Shekhinah, learned from Abraham in Genesis 18.

sources.ref: Tale of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi and his son Dov Ber

notes: The story's setting varies: some tellings have Dov Ber studying downstairs with the baby in the same room and Shneur Zalman upstairs in study or prayer. The outline says 'leaves his prayer'; the script says 'study and prayer'. Confirm the Chabad version and whose child it was (Dov Ber's).
Shabbat 127a (hospitality greater than receiving the Shekhinah) paraphrased; confirm.
'Saving a life comes before almost everything' is a general statement of pikuach nefesh; the script extends it to 'caring for someone in real need', which a Keeper may want to phrase differently.
